01 / THE BASIS

Build the return
into time.

Sines and cosines repeat. Combine harmonics with a shared period T, and both position and velocity meet at the seam. Try changing their amplitudes: the motion changes, the closure doesn’t.

d(t) = ∑ₖ aₖ sin(2πkt/T) + bₖ cos(2πkt/T)

A deterministic decoder of periodic time features is also periodic. Smooth velocity additionally needs a differentiable decoder. This toy uses the Fourier sum directly.

02 / THE SEAM

Same place.
Wrong speed.

“Same endpoints” adds a bump proportional to τ(1 − τ), where τ = t/T. The bump vanishes at both ends. Its velocity changes sign, so replaying the cycle introduces a kink.

Same endpoints ≠ a smooth seam

The diagnostics measure RMS 3D position and velocity differences across 120 ribbon angles. The chart shows one selected point’s horizontal displacement. Camera error is reported separately; it isn’t a pixel-quality score.

03 / THE NEW CONNECTION

Loop the scene,
then choose the shot.

OuroWorld (8 Oct 2026) fits multi-view generated motion with periodic 4D Gaussians. Its Fourier deformation field enforces loop closure; a separate reference-anchored drift field absorbs inconsistent training views.

The authors evaluate 39 scenes with static and ±20° orbit cameras, ground-truth-free metrics and a 30-person study. That does not establish unrestricted-view quality or physically correct motion. Official code ↗

What you’re looking at

840 hand-designed 3D Gaussians, analytic motion and a perspective covariance renderer. This is an explanation of periodicity, not OuroWorld inference, an implementation of its training procedure, or a benchmark. The “accumulated drift” toggle is a deliberately broken-loop example; it does not reproduce OuroWorld’s reference-anchored nuisance drift field. Fixed colors, approximate Gaussian falloff and center-depth alpha sorting simplify rendering. Periodicity guarantees a return, not a believable animation. A non-returning camera generally breaks the rendered loop even when the geometry is periodic.
